rationale: Internally consistent (MAX over a common danger scale with a negative expected sign is the correct mirror of the archive's MIN-over-safety construction) and the two legs are genuinely distinct channels, but this is now the fifth weakest-link/extremum specification in the archive, so the marginal information is mostly in the new legs rather than in the operator.

This is a mechanical rank-average of two signals already in the archive (ShortDebtFundingShortfallScaled and ShortfallDeterioration) with no new economic content, and averaging a strong-alpha level with a zero-alpha change will most likely dilute the level's portfolio evidence rather than reveal anything new.

The base quantity (dlc minus internal funds, scaled by assets) has already been tested in level, one-year-change and five-year-max form; substituting a five-year slope is a horizon variant of an existing signal rather than a substantively different mechanism.

Structurally sound conditional design (non-negative intensity rank times centered conditioner, sign matching the hypothesis) and it introduces the one distress axis the archive has never used, though both components — sales growth and cash-to-liabilities — are individually close to well-known published anomalies, so the test rests entirely on the interaction adding something beyond them.

The diagnosis of why the count version had a strong slope but zero alpha (integer ties plus a non-negative conditioner) is credible and the continuous fix is legitimate, but a five-year sum is close to five times the mean level of coverage and will be highly correlated with the current-level coverage measures already implicit in the archive, so the incremental content is modest.

Rescaling refinancing pressure by normalized earning power rather than assets is an economically motivated, non-cosmetic change with a well-argued near-always-positive denominator and a sign consistent with the expression; the main caveat is that net-short-debt-to-EBITDA is a standard credit metric, so it risks partly rediscovering the known (and weak) leverage effect.
